newsitem.title: DUBAI: Aramco dons business stripes in U.S. oil merger.
newsitem.headline: Aramco dons business stripes in U.S. oil merger.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's state oil giant Aramco will show further signs it can be a big player alongside Western majors on completing a merger of its U.S. downstream energy assets, Gulf economists and analysts said on Monday.
U.S. firms Texaco and Shell Oil Co said on Monday they were in talks aimed at merging their refining and retail operations in the U.S.
The tie up would include merging the assets of Texaco's joint venture with Saudi Aramco -- Star Enterprise -- and Shell Oil in the eastern U.S.

Faced with depressed operating margins in the competitive U.S. market, Aramco has apparently been won over by the need to rationalise to secure future profitability in the world's biggest petroleum consumer market.

Though it is cushioned by enviable access to the world's largest oil reserves and is free from shareholder demands, Aramco rarely takes on the guise of the slow political animal which characterises other nationalised oil firms elsewhere.
"Aramco could be a listed on any equity market and be unrecognisable from the likes of Exxon...profits are the bottom line," one Gulf based analyst said.
Economists in the region said former Aramco head Ali Ibrahim Naimi, who last year replaced his long-serving predecessor Hisham Nazer, typified Aramco's business ethic.
"Naimi is not a political creation...He does his job which is to maximise the country's revenue," one analyst at a Western oil company based in the kingdom said.
The Dhahran-based firm has been at the forefront of creating marketing alliances with foreign firms to gain access to guaranteed retail markets in exchange for supplying crude oil to the refineries.

Since the late 1980s, Aramco has outpaced its colleagues in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and tied up downstream deals in South Korea, Philippines and Greece in addition to its first venture which was the U.S. in 1989.
Then Aramco teamed up with Texaco to form Star Enterprise which allows Riyadh to place 600,000 barrels per day (bpd) of its output of eight million bpd directly to the U.S. pump.

Star and other foreign ventures already soak up some 1.5 million bpd of Saudi crude and Aramco aims to clinch deals in China, India and Portugal so that more of its exports are shielded from international oil price volatility.
The U.S-Saudi Star venture owns three refineries in Texas, Louisiana and Delaware and incorporates some 9,000 service stations in eastern U.S.
Aramco already has a working relationship with Shell in Saudi Arabia where the two companies are partners in an oil export refinery at Jubail on the northern Gulf coast.
Shell also has extensive interests in Saudi Arabia's growing petrochemical sector.

British Petroleum Plc and Mobil Corp announced in February that they were planning to merge their European downstream assets to save some $500 million a year in pretax savings by cutting overheads and duplication.

Saudi Arabia's current economic plan for 1995-2000 mandates the company to achieve a higher level of integration and "participation in the ownership of oil refineries and marketing outlets in major markets."
